label: rem:meridian-exceptional-divisor-note
title: The meridian is at the exceptional divisor; the per-operation tick is the Compton time, not the Planck time
html:
Physically, the meridian is a 1-cycle in the exceptional-divisor fibre \mathcal{S}_p: after the base coordinate hits the discriminant and the smooth base pinches, the cusp torus and its meridian are the geometry of \mathcal{S}_p. So the statement "the meridian is at the exceptional divisor" is literal, and by the boost identity one meridian turn — one knot operation — is a hyperbolic rotation of rapidity \ln q_0 \approx 0.104 along the bar-odd (Chern–Simons) axis, the same axis along which the cusp shape sits (\mathrm{barOdd}(\omega)^2 = -3).

This fixes the natural time per operation, and it is not the Planck time. A rotation is dimensionless; converting it to a duration divides by an energy, t = \hbar / E, and the substrate energy scale is m_e (the leptonic calibration CAL-1). The per-operation tick is therefore the electron Compton time

  t_C = \hbar / (m_e c^2) \approx 1.29 \times 10^{-21}\ \text{s},

which is \sim 22 orders of magnitude longer than the Planck time t_P \approx 5.39 \times 10^{-44} s. The ratio is exactly m_{\mathrm{Planck}} / m_e \approx 2.4 \times 10^{22} — the gravitational hierarchy, a standard measured quantity built from \hbar, c, G, m_e and owing nothing to this framework.

Identifying the computational tick with the Planck time would pin the substrate at m_{\mathrm{Planck}}, i.e. introduce Newton's constant G — an input outside the three-calibration weak sector (m_e, P_{\mathrm{skew}}^{\beta}, P_{\mathrm{avg}}^{\pi}). That is a fourth calibration and a substrate-scale derivation, which the framework does not undertake. The honest per-operation tick is the Compton / electroweak time; the 22-order gap to gravity is not something the framework predicts, and by construction it need not.
